This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a maximum likelihood estimator can be used to accurately estimate parameters of this newly developed model. We also established the asymptotic properties of the estimator, specifically that it is statistically consistent and normally distributed. To apply this model effectively in real-world scenarios, we have developed an easy-to-implement algorithm for estimating its variance. Furthermore, we have conducted a simulation experiment to evaluate the model's performance, demonstrating its ability to accurately forecast counts and identify changes in underlying patterns. A real-data example is also provided to illustrate the model's practical utility in analyzing and forecasting airline passenger data.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions.

Numerous numerical methods have been developed to resolve the stochastic forces in biomolecular models, with some employing simple Gaussian distributions and others using more complex simulations to re-establish equilibrium. Our research introduces a novel, straightforward method called 'Residual Re-simulation' (RR) that exploits existing force calculations to re-simulate the displaced atomic configurations, found to be highly effective in achieving equilibrium. Through extensive testing on a variety of biochemical processes, including protein and DNA systems, RR outperforms the simple Gaussian restoration of forces in nearly all cases, with significant improvements in accuracy in situations where more complex simulations are necessary to re-establish equilibrium. Furthermore, RR's efficiency makes it ideal for use in molecular dynamics simulations that employ temperature control, as it reduces the thermal fluctuations that can disrupt biochemical events. Based on the results, RR offers a simple and effective approach for biomolecular modeling, demonstrating substantial gains in conformational averaging accuracy over simple Gaussian restoration of forces, while also simplifying the more complex re-establishment of equilibrium simulations.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability is compromised when using such externally sourced data, as it may not accurately reflect the system's performance in real-world scenarios. To address this issue, an unbiased performance evaluation method is proposed that utilizes the in-built description capability of eye-tracking systems. This method allows for the objective evaluation of automatic image description systems on videos of everyday activities, as it generates natural, human-like descriptions in real-time. This approach enables the assessment of systems based on their accuracy in describing actions and their corresponding outcomes, as well as their overall quality, which can vary depending on factors such as system performance and image quality.

Quantum field theory, particularly in 1+1 dimensions, has seen significant developments through the study of conformal field theories and their connections to state and complexity. This review focuses on underlying principles and recent findings in this area of research. A key chapter explores the underlying physics and gauge/gravity duality implications of the "holographic" mass-volume linear relationship observed in certain theories. A second chapter delves into the applications of CFTs in understanding both the complexity of quantum states and the complexity operator interrelation in 1+1 dimensional physics. Recent breakthroughs have also been summarized, including the discovery of non-linear complexity relationships and the advent of new geometric tools such as the bulk Nambu-Goto framework. A final chapter examines the current state of CFT models and theoretical frameworks, along with suggestions for future research directions.

The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC.

This research paper investigates the performance of SISO-OFDM and a newly proposed MISO-OFDM video streaming system over satellite links. It presents three different transmitter configurations: a widely used MISO-OFDM scheme, an optimized MISO-OFDM method, and a newly proposed MISO-OFDM technique that utilizes joint optimization of precoding matrices and symbol extensions. Our proposed method offers improved performance by jointly optimizing precoding matrices and symbol extensions compared to the widely used MISO-OFDM scheme. It also outperforms the optimized MISO-OFDM method as it considers additional variables. Our research found that the proposed scheme provides better performance when compared to other satellite video streaming systems but incurs higher computational costs. Our proposed scheme provides better performance when compared to other satellite video streaming systems but incurs higher computational costs. Our results show that our proposed scheme achieves higher throughput with less error occurrence. It also meets technical requirements for video streaming as per the specified bit-rate values.

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies.

This study undertakes a linear stability analysis of a flame, incorporating both heat release fluctuations and noise, using a simplified model. The aim is to investigate how dust explosion ignition, in a vented enclosure, influences acoustic fluctuations and resulting noise. To analyze these effects, five different linear stability flux diagrams are computed, each representing a specific frequency of noise. The "bistability" phenomenon is observed, where increasing the stability of a flame leads to reduced noise, but also decreases the threshold for instability in a different frequency range. An analogy is drawn between the stability flux diagrams and a simple electrical RLC circuit, illustrating the "bistability" as a proof of the Bistable RLC Circuit Model. The results suggest that the most stable flux diagram corresponds to the most stable RLC circuit configuration, with both involving resonance at a specific frequency. The Bistable RLC Circuit Model is supported by experimental data, demonstrating the effectiveness of the electrical circuit analogy in understanding dust explosion-induced noise and flame stability in a vented enclosure.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent integral connection. We present an extended version of the theory where the integral connection is free from specific restrictions. The derived nonlocal gravity theory shows consistency with the established framework and offers novel insights. The source term in the history-dependent integral can be seen as a new field, and its dynamics are determined. The theory's predictive power is demonstrated by showing that it reduces to traditional Einstein gravity in specific cases.

This paper discusses recent findings from the LHC involving small systems studied
by the ALICE, ATLAS and CMS collaborations. Due to the growing importance
of QCD in small systems, particularly in situations with high multiplicity, not
all significant results can be covered in this report. It primarily focuses on
P-P and A-A Aale Ph geometry and collective dynamics in small systems, plus
selected results on open and hidden charm production. The underlying intention
is to provide a comprehensive summary of key findings from the 2022 QCD-18 meeting.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that their outburst recurrence times do not follow the established pattern seen in low mass X-ray binary neutron star systems. However, recent discoveries of a highly recurrent and a moderately recurrent neutron star binary in the LMC have now challenging this claim. The most recurrent of these binaries, with a recurrence time of just 90 days, has an mass of about 1.4 solar masses, and its angular momentum is not sufficient to spin back up the star during accretion. This leaves only a narrow range of possible masses and compositions for the remaining 95% of neutron stars, and suggests that the majority of those that form in binary systems will not contain a second neutron star if the maximum mass of 2 solar masses is the limit above which stars collapse into black holes. This limit is supported by the observed recurrence times of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intense, leading to the desire for algorithms that can handle this task approximately. Unlike general graphs, some bipartite graphs, known as pseudo-regular graphs, have a specific edge-crossing number of zero, implying their complete representation is theoretically possible. Nevertheless, determining if a given pseudo-regular graph has zero edge-crossing number is notoriously difficult, with no polynomial-time algorithm available for solving the problem. Despite this challenge, our research introduces an approximate edge-crossing reduction method for bipartite graphs, which we call the "Step Back, Move Forward" (SBMF) algorithm, that builds upon a initial random edge crossing arrangement. This algorithm iteratively applies a series of local optimizations to edge crossings, allowing for significant time savings by reducing the problem size, although directly not decreasing edge crossings directly. Our findings demonstrate the SBMF algorithm consistently outperforms existing alternatives in various test scenarios on both large-scale pseudo-regular graphs and real-world bipartite data sets, showcasing its potential for visualizing complex connections on a screen. Furthermore, our research includes additional results showing the SBMF algorithm's ability to reduce edge crossings in a separate variant of the problem known as the minimum edge

In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, HyperDegrade, which incorporates previous methods and employs simultaneous multithreading architectures.  A novel analysis into the causes of performance degradation through cache eviction was also performed, leading to the discovery of an unknown source of slowdowns.  Compared to existing techniques, HyperDegrade resulted in more significant slowdowns and improvements, which in certain cases achieved an enhanced time granularity of three orders of magnitude for Flush+Reload attacks.  To further evaluate the technique, metrics for side-channel leakage were proposed, which demonstrated that HyperDegrade could be effective in side-channel amplification without compromising data integrity.  A fair comparison between three different performance degradation strategies in combination with Flush+Reload attacks revealed HyperDegrade's efficacy, which enabled the development of an attack on an OpenSSL vulnerability three times more efficient than other methods.  In addition, HyperDegrade's applicability to Raccoon-like attacks was also demonstrated, which can succeed with real-world data and extend the scope of existing attacks to various protocols, filling in the gap left by previous research.

A localized alteration in knot diagrams is referred to as an unknotting operation. It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram, although the minimum number of unknotting moves required for this conversion is not necessarily the most straightforward. A more significant contribution of this study is that any knot diagram can be transformed into a state of connected component consisting of a single loop through a sequence of unknotting operations, without generating any new variations in the process, and without altering the overall component structure.

In multi-agent systems where cooperation is not guaranteed, a strategy profile is considered trustworthy for completing tasks if it leads to a Nash equilibrium with all agents receiving their desired outcomes. However, calculating Nash equilibria can be computationally complex, even for simple systems. A new approach has been developed, combining shallow neural networks and a closed-form equilibrium predictor, dubbed as NeuralEQ, to efficiently accomplish complex tasks and enable trustworthy coordination.

A recurring theme in combinatorial group theory is the intricate relationship between various product operations, specifically the direct product, centralizer, and the wreath product. Building upon the established facts that the centralizer of a subgroup in a group and the subgroup itself are interrelated through a wreath product, we have derived an explicit isomorphism between their commutator subgroups. This isomorphism is symbolically represented as a diagram, illustrating the interconnectedness of these subgroups and products.

This research aims to examine and evaluate various technical constraints that limit the sensitivity of advanced gravitational-wave detectors in the high-frequency range. Optical spring telemetry vulnerabilities, radiation pressure noise, and quantum limitations of light sources are key areas of consideration. To better understand these constraints, the paper delves into detailed theoretical analyses of both the closed-loop squeezing sideband removal technique and the quantum noise performance of radiation pressure detection, with a focus on high-frequency range optimization. Additionally, the study explores possible solutions, including using closed-loop squeezing to reduce noise and employing correlated quantum noises to mitigate limitations. The research further involves calculating and modeling various parameters to assess the optical coherence rejection modulation's effectiveness in eliminating noise. The primary goal is to predict the overall sensitivity that advanced detectors can achieve in the high-frequency range through improved source-light quantum noise reduction.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems with a significant number of antennas exhibit a shift towards a scale that is massive. Implementing such a system as a single entity is impractical, thus the idea of distributed extra-large scale MIMO systems has been proposed. This research investigates the feasibility of using distributed extra-large scale MIMO systems in densely populated environments with a high number of users. The findings suggest that both narrowband and wideband systems can achieve significant gains in signal strength through the exploitation of multiplexing gains and the application of iterative decoding methods. The results also indicate that the performance of both systems is significantly enhanced when using a combination of wideband MIMO systems and large-scale small cells.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to train models on large datasets. Our approach offers enhanced language knowledge through the $n$-gram base model, eliminating the need for massive computational requirements and enabling the model to accurately predict words in context. Our method, dubbed the "Residual Neural $n$-gram" model, resulted in impressive outcomes when tested on standard language tasks and data sets, outperforming the initial combination of neural and $n$-gram models and demonstrating substantial potential for neural $n$-gram models, especially in sparse data scenarios.

This research seeks to address the challenges of inaccurate optical character recognition (OCR) and exploits its potential by introducing an Informed OCR (IoOCR) system, which utilizes metadata from the source document to improve the accuracy of OCR. An experimental framework was designed and implemented to evaluate the effectiveness of IoOCR in the context of document-based applications, targeting both general-purpose and special-purpose OCR systems. The results indicate that IoOCR consistently outperforms traditional OCR systems and demonstrates superior performance in various scenarios. The research reveals that an ideal IoOCR system would resemble the underlying text generation process, and in cases of perfectly accurate OCR, it would mirror the source document's structure. The findings suggest that IoOCR systems are more resilient to OCR errors compared to conventional OCR systems and exhibit improved performance in applications involving document classification, sentiment analysis, and named entity recognition. The data presented in Table III highlights the efficacy of IoOCR in enhancing OCR accuracy, and the proposed IoOCR framework offers promising potential for future research.

A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation speeds and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which various global atmospheric patterns emerge or disappear. Multiple jet stream patterns can form when the rotation speed or temperature difference increases, and the models predict that a slow rotation speed allows for a single jet stream while a faster speed allows for multiple jet stream patterns. Existing theoretical knowledge on the topic is found to be incomplete, and new insights are gained on how rotation speed, planetary temperature, and jet stream patterns are interconnected.

This study formulates a genuine integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function in terms of a modified hypersingular integral. It also derives a representation involving a modified hypersingular integral for the logarithmic derivative of the gamma function.

Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this study, we've developed a novel stochastic differential equation expansion of the positive-P phase-space formalism, specifically designed to study interacting Bose gases within the framework of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation.  Our newly derived equation, which we call the second-order extended hydrodynamic approach, demonstrates significant improvements over existing positive-P methods, exhibiting enhanced accuracy and significantly reduced statistical errors, particularly when analyzing collective rotation excitations.  Using this new equation, we've resolved a long-standing issue associated with the first-order Anisimov-Borrére-Alexandrov (AB1) method concerning the correct calculation of absolute absolute quantum vortices dynamics, and have successfully simulated a harmonic potential release scenario, demonstrating the method's ability to accurately describe the formation of vortices and vortex lattices.  Our results demonstrate the positive-P phase-space formalism's potential to simulate genuine quantum many-body dynamics, and we anticipate its utility in a wide range of quantum many-body research areas.

Deep neural networks have experienced significant growth in various domains, making them challenging to train, thereby leading to the Teacher-Student architecture, where the knowledge learned by the student network is derived from a previously trained or known teacher model. Initially employed in spoken language recognition and low-resource languages, Teacher-Student architectures have gained popularity and are now utilized in knowledge distillation for various purposes, including regularizing students through temperature adjustment, using extra teacher models, and employing multi-layer peer models. Currently, these architectures are applied across a wide range of networks in various domains, making them a cornerstone of knowledge distillation. In addition, the theoretical foundations of Teacher-Student architectures have been established, providing a framework for understanding their functionality and optimizing their performance.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our deterministic finite state automata function module, dubbed mdfa, exceeds the capabilities of standard matrix-based representations and conditional random fields for modeling complex functions. Our mdfa implementation outperforms mdfa's theoretical advantages by being easily learned from vast amounts of contextual embedding data, with mdfa often matching or surpassing the performance of conditional random fields in our experimental results. Our conditional random field model using mdfa, titled cfw, demonstrates superior performance compared to conditional random fields and conditional linear flow models in tackling structured prediction tasks, with cfw exceeding the performance of conditional random fields in our experimental outcomes. Our conditional random field model using mdfa, titled cfw, exhibits improved performance over conditional random fields and conditional linear flow models in handling structured prediction tasks, with cwf showing comparable performance to conditional linear flow models in our experimental findings.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, particularly with respect to a specific embedding of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within a tensor product. As a result, the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be presented through generators and defining relations, offering an innovative perspective on its structure. Additionally, the series known as the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be computed explicitly. The research presented addresses the issue of describing the centralizer $Z_{3}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ completely, in both its algebraic and geometric forms, thereby providing a novel solution to the problem.

This study develops an efficient natural language processing system for testing if there's a significant statistical dependence between two sets of variables. This system's key distinguishing feature is its ability to identify subtle connections between specific language phenomena, enabling the analysis of complex interactions such as context-dependent suppletive morphology shifts in languages like French. We have designed two primary applications for this system: a machine learning-based evaluation demonstrating its efficiency in accurately identifying dependent relationships in a large data set, and a symbolic computation evaluation that confirms the system's capability to detect known information about a specific language, along with newly discovered information.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles.

This research develops a novel, Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are organized on a grid. A streamlined variation of the Rao-Blackwellized particle filter applies to a subset of grid points, allowing for efficient management of multiple target identities. Unlike conventional Gaussian mixture models, this grid-based approach effectively curbs the growth of state space dimensions, preventing the occurrence of duplicate identities and reducing metabolic overhead. Furthermore, to enhance filter accuracy, a targeted version of the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm updates grid point particle representations. Evaluations using simulated data demonstrate the effectiveness of the grid-based PMBM filter in tracking multiple targets with rapid movements, outperforming both the standard Gaussian mixture model approach and a widely used alternative known as the joint multi-Bernoulli filter.

The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can significantly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can quickly determine the best action to increase the chance of scoring and reducing the opponent's scoring chances in advanced soccer systems. Our approach demonstrates excellent performance in simulated environments and real-world data, showing promise for improving team performance on the field.

The surge in telework and remote learning has created opportunities for individuals to engage in unique scientific studies from anywhere in the world. We developed and demonstrated a two-dimensional Laser Doppler Vibrometry system using a single-input multiple-output (SIMO) graphical processing unit (GPU) acoustic laser system, capable of simultaneously analyzing and imaging the acoustic vibration patterns of sample areas. Our system enables rapid, wide-area resonance frequency mapping of thin film samples, allowing for the identification of distinct vibration regions and calculation of corresponding resonance frequencies. Our data shows that our two-dimensional Laser Doppler Vibrometry system can effectively detect even slight vibrations induced by sound waves and locally applied forces, and can accurately determine resonance frequencies of thin film samples within a wide frequency range. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of using our two-dimensional Laser Doppler Vibrometry system to visually represent the structural characteristics of thin film samples, including the detection of lamellar boundaries, determination of film thickness, and identification of mechanical resonance modes of individual lamellae.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a detailed analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

In experiments involving particle collisions, identifying neutral long-lived particles relies on either finding decay products at large distances or missing energy. The choice between these methods depends on the particle's properties, as well as those of the detector used. To better understand the effectiveness of these methods, we are examining how they complement each other, with a focus on Belle II's searches for axion-like particles through the $B^+ 	o K^+ E_i{}/$ decay process. To optimize both searches for these particles, we are developing a unified theoretical framework that takes into account the production and detection of neutral, long-lived particles, including the relevant physical processes and factors influencing them. This includes calculations of particle lifespans, detection probabilities, and the sensitivity of Belle II's experiments to detect these particles, as well as the inclusion of relevant theoretical uncertainties. Based on this framework, we are predicting the sensitivity that Belle II's Belle II experiment will have in detecting axion-like particles with a mass of 10 GeV, assuming a production rate of 10^12 neutral particles per square centimeter. On the other hand, we are also predicting the sensitivity that Belle II's experiment will have in detecting these particles via the decay of neutral particles into visible products, as well as the detection of visible products in conjunction with the presence of missing energy, assuming a production rate of 10^12 neutral particles per square centimeter.

This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized, along with
 suggestions for future research on the category of mass nouns, noun class
 changes, and the challenges of automatizing semantic change detection.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research employs a novel, unified approach to accurately determine the masses and spins of two AGNs, Fairall SPHERICAL GALAXY 09 and Mrk 766. Using radio to ultraviolet data and a state-of-the-art accretion disk model, the General Relativistic Consistent Picture, the team calculates the masses to be approximately 2 x 10^9 times that of the solar mass and around 8 x 10^6 times that of the solar mass for Fairall SPHERICAL GALAXY 09 and Mrk 766 respectively. Additionally, the team finds the spin parameters to be near the maximum possible value of 0.98 for both AGNs, and the accretion disk temperatures to be significantly enhanced due to the strong spin-induced gravitational redshift. This research provides strong evidence that certain AGNs feature black holes with large spin values, thereby supporting certain theoretical models, including superradiation and the formation of jet relativistic cores.

A quantum harmonic oscillator's quantum states can be defined and visualized in a shape that resembles a classical harmonic oscillator. When a quantum harmonic oscillator is placed in a state with a specific quantum number, it resembles a classical oscillator with significant amplitude. However, when the oscillator is in a coherent state, due to its wide spread of quantum levels, it resembles a classical oscillator with constant motion. When a quantum harmonic oscillator is subjected to constant forces, it behaves similarly to a classical oscillator as well as a free quantum particle, as it allows for the transition between these two states.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, demonstrating how pre-existing programs can be logically linked, the existing precision theorem can be re-proved, and a new program that can opt for reliable versus efficient program behaviour can be verified.

This study examines the sources of bias in estimating the perpendicular component of the magnetic field from vector magnetograms. We use a synthetic data set generated from local temperature monochromatic observations, assuming a constant heliocentric angle of 30 degrees. The set includes 20 noiseless magnetograms and their corresponding local photosurface velocity data, as well as a representative observational data set from local bipolar jet observations. All components of the vector magnetic field are recoverable with high accuracy except for the perpendicular component, which shows a significant bias. This research finds that the main contributor to this bias is a combination of transverse shear velocities and the polarimetric measurement limit of about 20 mas per pixel. Additionally, the study finds that the heliocentric angle has a minor effect on this bias. A faster transverse shear velocity results in a more substantial bias, and the ideal recovery threshold is approximately 10 km/s. A fitting model predicts the optimal retaking strategy: sacrificing area to boost pixel sensitivity or using faster velocities as costs are balanced. A total of 20 noiseless data sets with varying shear velocities are used to determine the optimal retaking curve that balances area and sensitivity for different situations. A universal retaking curve is proposed for the Euclidean decomposition method, which serves as a guideline for vector inversion code developers and observers.

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that it resembles a collection of indistinguishable components that are each equivalent to a sphere. Specifically, when the group's underlying set has a dimension of d, we demonstrate that such a boolean complex is equivalent to a combination of (0)d+1)-dimensional spheres that are indistinguishable. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to calculate the number of components as well as the overall complex's volume for finite Coxeter groups.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, as different loss functions are suited to different types of data. Despite this, many deep learning applications employ a limited range of loss functions, primarily centered on the idea of minimizing the difference between predicted and actual outcomes. In the majority of cases, loss function optimization is achieved through the application of established, pre-derived loss values, often obtained from previous studies or generic initialization methods. In contrast, this research seeks to reframe the loss function as a parameter that requires direct optimization, analogous to the network's weights and bias. The study demonstrates that by applying a loss function in its unoptimized, initial state can lead to suboptimal results, thereby necessitating its optimization before use. This discovery underscores the significance of selecting an appropriate loss function, as it serves as a foundation for training the network. Furthermore, the research introduces the concept of loss function matching, which involves carefully selecting loss functions that are suitable for specific data types to ensure optimal performance.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules consisting of 1 million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that enables machine learning models to reason effectively about cause-and-effect relationships.  Our research highlights the significance of contextual information in commonsense reasoning, as seen in the example: "I cut myself, and I feel pain because I inflicted an injury on myself," which illustrates how models should focus on the causal relationship between cutting themselves and the resulting pain, rather than the act of cutting itself.  Our dataset evaluation involves presenting models with a variety of contextual information scenarios to assess their ability to apply established rules and learn new ones through few-shot learning.  Our results demonstrate that by incorporating the default contextual information associated with action verbs into models, we can enhance commonsense reasoning about everyday situations.  Our findings suggest that intent can be accurately determined from the structure of conditional relationships, which enables zero-shot learning for newly discovered rules.  Our research provides a comprehensive foundation for investigating how artificial intelligence models can develop commonsense reasoning capabilities through the application of commonsense knowledge.

This research presents a novel, video-level view transformation prediction model. It utilizes both temporal and spatial information in novel videos, as well as the characteristics of existing videos. Our proposed network consists of two components: a novel view generator and a view recognition module. The first component uses existing videos to predict novel videos through an iterative process, incorporating spatial and temporal attention mechanisms to ensure accurate prediction. The second component uses predicted novel videos to identify the current view of the robot, employing a convolutional neural network and a recurrent neural network to analyze the environment and robot's movement. We evaluated our model on two large-scale datasets: Robot Navigation and Airless. On the Robot Navigation dataset, our model achieved the highest accuracy at 90 degrees, outperforming the current state-of-the-art by 10 percentage points. On the Airless dataset, our model showed the best performance at 120 degrees, surpassing the existing best by 20 percentage points.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we explore the opposite idea: how identifiable should a set of vertices R remain in a modified graph that has been affected by some changes? This is referred to as the "lasting dimension" of the graph. We examine various scenarios of change including additions, removals, and modifications of vertices and present efficient identifying sets in various types of graphs to determine how resilient they are to change.

Early detection of heart ailments is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, we propose a robust, real-time cardiac abnormality detection system called Noise-Aware Cardiac Abnormality Detection (NCAD).  This system utilizes a deep learning-based approach and incorporates information about noise levels in recorded sounds, significantly enhancing detection accuracy.  We evaluated NCAD on two publicly available datasets: PhysioNet-COVID and APTN.  Compared to existing methods, NCAD demonstrated superior performance when using cheap, built-in microphones in devices like smart speakers, resulting in high sensitivity (99.2%) and specificity (97.6%) on the APTN dataset.  The NCAD system also demonstrated practical value by reducing error rates in combination with existing cardiac imaging techniques on large datasets like MedTesta (96.2% sensitivity, 97.4% specificity) and ClinicalTesta (98.6% sensitivity, 96.3% specificity).  Our findings suggest that NCAD offers a cost-effective, point-of-care solution for detecting heart abnormalities using smart speakers and existing imaging techniques.

We examined the relationship between the gas and stellar masses of galaxies for 650 local 2MAEGS sources, incorporating both the standard assumption of local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) and a newly identified issue with non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) excitation of carbon lines. We found that the gas mass fraction declined as the stellar mass increased when using both LTE and non-LTE conditions, although the non-LTE scenario yielded a shallower slope. Additionally, we discovered that the gas temperature derived from non-LTE excitation of carbon lines is lower than that from the LTE assumption, which led to a more gradual slope when using non-LTE conditions. However, both approaches with both conditions failed to account for the gas mass fraction at low stellar masses, which could be attributed to the onset of star formation or the presence of high-redshift galaxies. We also explored the relationship between the gas and stellar masses of galaxies for four different observational datasets, finding that the gas mass fraction declined as the stellar mass increased when using both LTE and non-LTE conditions, although the non-LTE scenario yielded a more gradual slope in two out of four cases.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process.

This paper examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy. We begin by investigating the optimal control of basic reproductive numbers for the Kermack-McKendrick models to determine the strategies that minimize virus spread. Subsequently, we analyze the dynamics of contact networks in a structured population to reevaluate the strategies mentioned earlier. Moreover, we modify the previous scenarios to account for different contact network structures. Finally, we evaluate the effectiveness of strategies that involve reducing virus transmission risk in certain population groups.

Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To examine the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study was conducted on 6500 local star-forming galaxies observed by the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. Over 70% of these galaxies have an active star-formulating disk and a mature existing bulge. This research found a strong link between bulge mass and Sersic index, indicating more massive bulges form earlier. As a result, galaxies with more massive bulges and a higher Sersic index generally form stars more slowly, appearing at the low-specific star formation end of the main sequence. However, no sudden transition was observed when converting from normal to slow star formation rates on the main sequence. Instead, this rate transitions smoothly as a function of bulge mass and Sersic index, suggesting a steady influence of bulges on the main sequence rather than a discrete boundary. Moreover, the mass function of bulges mirrors the main sequence, allowing for an alternative interpretation: galaxies with slow star formation rates simply host larger bulges, which in turn deposit their formed stars more slowly into the center of the galaxy, further slowing star formation in the disk. Therefore, the leading hypothesis is that the extended presence of massive stars resulting from previous star formation in bulges fuels slower star formation in adjacent disks, leading to an inverted U shape when plotting specific star formation rate against bulge mass.

This research conducts sentiment analysis on English language tweets without utilizing a labeled dataset. It utilizes a combination of three annotated datasets (Affective Norms, Sentiment Lexicons, and a Semantics Pilot Dataset) to develop a sentiment prediction model. The proposed approach consists of an initial step with a pre-trained language model to predict sentiment, followed by a further refinement using a supervised machine learning model on a subset of the highest confidence predictions. The research employs multiple sentiment categories and utilizes a pre-trained language model as the base model. The findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, indicating that sentiment analysis can be accurately performed using a single dataset with a high confidence prediction.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Finally, we explored possible explanations for this strange internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observations to confirm our findings.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid spread and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been effective in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their performance significantly deteriorates when dealing with emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a completely new detection system from scratch, as previously trained models are not applicable, adds to the challenge. To address this issue, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module for handling multiple information sources, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by processing information in an incremental and structured manner. The system MetaFEND has been tested and evaluated on three different datasets (i.e., COVID-19, HeartDisease, and FEVER725) and has achieved impressive results.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding. This research extends the idea of Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays. A new construction method for pairs of complementary arrays is introduced, as well as an algorithm to generate all possible pairs. It is demonstrated that the NT degree of a lattice $\Lambda$ in higher-dimensional spaces is a suitable criterion for identifying possible pair sizes. The research extends previous results on pairs of complementary arrays in one-dimensional spaces and derives new fundamental bounds. It also presents examples of feasible array sizes based on an ideal lattice in a 4-dimensional Euclidean space and a lattice with linear form in a 6-dimensional Euclidean space.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific part of the brain, and our research aims to develop an advanced imaging technique to effectively monitor this procedure.  A mathematical model was created to simulate the brain's temperature changes during the LITT treatment, and based on this model, we developed an optimization algorithm to precisely control the LITT treatment and ensure it meets the desired therapeutic standards.  Our optimized strategy outperformed the current standard of care in a variety of scenarios, and it is compatible with standard brain imaging techniques, demonstrating its potential to significantly improve the effectiveness of LITT treatment.  Our findings provide a valuable framework for improving LITT treatment and its potential to benefit patients suffering from epilepsy and their treating physicians.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. One widely used method is contrastive learning, which we have enhanced with an aspect known as local contrast of contrastive learning techniques. Our novel approach, titled LocalContrast, incorporates contrastive learning to efficiently extract valuable features.  LocalContrence learns to highlight distinctive aspects of data through contrastive optimization, and then employs a standard CNN to capture these aspects as valuable features.  Our localized contrast approach allows for real-time learning and reduces computational complexity.  Our LocalContrence method outperformed existing contrastive learning techniques in terms of performance, according to metric scores, and also demonstrated superior performance in real-world data sets, according to classification accuracy.  Our localized contrast approach allowed for real-time feature extraction as localContrence learned quickly to demonstrate impressive results in real-world data sets, according to classification accuracy. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. To further enhance the capabilities of these models, researchers are exploring the integration of structured knowledge from knowledge graphs into these models. One promising approach is to train models on descriptive sentences generated from knowledge graphs, which has shown promise in generating effective knowledge-based representations. However, the challenge of choosing appropriate context lies within the integrated representation. In our proposed method, we leverage the inherent structure of knowledge graphs to create context that allows the model to generate the desired representation directly. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on large language models and present evidence that it outperforms both the generation of descriptive sentences and the use of natural language instructions. Our findings indicate that pre-trained models can learn to generate representations that excel in knowledge-based tasks at the level of the best reported results.

A novel approach has been proposed to investigate the phase transition temperature in black holes by utilizing the shadow radius rather than the horizon radius. This method is grounded in the integrated accretion disk temperature, being sensitive to subtle changes at the first-order phase transition. Within the framework of Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity, we examine the QNME (quasi-normal modal evolution) approach and the accretion disk semi-analytical method to verify the phase transition transition through shadow or image radius changes. Furthermore, we computated the shadow radius $r_{s}$ explicitly in different scenarios of phase transition, confirming it aligns with the deconfinement phase transition temperature. The EGBC model with specific parameters exhibits a second order phase transition at $\bar{\gamma} \approx 0.45$, while the phase transition temperature varies directly with $\kappa_{A}$ and inversely with $\gamma_{c}$. Lastly, we examined the relation between shadow radius and decay time in different phases of a black hole.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed recently for state reconstruction from an optical tomogram, incorporating both homodyne and heterodyne measurements, though they are often cumbersome and require sophisticated technical setups. In contrast, a simple method to reconstruct a state's non-classical properties from an optical tomogram has been developed recently using the Gaussian transformation and feedback process with cooperating particles. Here, we extend that approach by distilling a simple protocol to extract a Wigner function from an optical tomogram through a single Raman scattering event with a cooperating particle.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also collected data on the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, within a specific energy range of 14 TeV proton-proton collisions at a particle accelerator. The research team has developed a new method for measuring the time difference between the decay of a particle and its subsequent decay product. Based on this method, they have measured the branching fractions for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay modes, as well as other related fractions. The measured branching fractions for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay modes are 4.3+0.5-0.4 x 10^-4 and 1.8+0.4-0.3 x 10^-4, respectively, following two standard errors of their estimated values. The research findings are consistent with predictions made by theoretical models, and have contributed to a better understanding of the strong force's properties.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the practical value of this task, only a few specific cases have lattice descriptions established due to the overwhelming complexity of general modules. However, for modules that are direct sums of simple modules, a recursive method exists to construct their lattice of submodules, based on the lattice of submodules of the individual simple modules, which are relatively straightforward to map. Although this approach is theoretically viable, its applicability is limited by the need to determine the composition factors of each submodule, which can be extremely difficult to pinpoint for many modules. To circumvent this challenge, we propose an alternative approach that focuses on finding join irreducible submodules of a given module, which serve as the building blocks to construct its lattice of submodules. This description can then be used to visualize the lattice in a meaningful manner. Moreover, we outline the steps to compute the lattice of submodules of a module $M$ as an algebraic system, whose input consists of a set of representative join irreducible submodules of $M$ along with their join operations.

We explore how several established recurrent operators including curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators contribute significantly to biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal within the Euclidean space.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the shape of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate is determined as a function of hadron recoil. This rate is reconstructed via the $D_s^{-}$ decay into $K^-K^+\pi^-$, following the $D_s^{*-}$ decay into $D_s^{-}\gamma$. The resulting rate is fit with CLN and BGL form factor parametrisations to derive key parameters for both models.

A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics using both the Lyapunov exponent and a consistently observed multi-folded mapping of the pattern variation. Additionally, we observe the correlation dimension plateauing at a value of 1 within the typical range of stretching forces, indicating a deterministic source of the signal. Therefore, we conclude that these dynamics are truly chaotic and not stochastic, discounting the validity of previous analyses.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems the underlying structure for these problems. Within this framework of space with betweenness properties, the article has solved the initial illumination problem and the tiling problem after it has been reformulated.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive applications but require retraining when faced with new viewpoints.  A majority of research has focused on individual transformations and isn't comprehensive in categorizing all possible changes.  A new framework, called TPC, has been proposed that involves three sub-models, each addressing a specific type of transformation: global, local, and composite.  The TPC framework achieves impressive results with fewer training samples needed for each new transformation than the existing methods.  By utilizing the TPC framework with popular point cloud models, researchers found that they could train models that require 10 times less data when shifting from 2D images to point clouds and also learned from real-world data with domain adaptation.  The best-performing model, named PointContrast, achieved top-1 accuracy of 90.3% on the ModelNet40 dataset.  The PointContrast model outperformed existing methods when tested on ten different datasets including the Scene11K and the SunRGBD datasets and also demonstrated significant performance boosts in real-world experiments with a robotic arm.

A growing body of research has integrated formal methods with testing to enhance program reliability. A key challenge in leveraging this combination is determining suitable test cases that formal verification can validate. A newly proposed framework, called ValiTest, exploits the potential for both formal verification and testing to guarantee safety-critical properties hold for all executable code. A safety property is defined as a reachability claim, specifying the program should reach a particular state within a certain time if given certain inputs. Once a property is established, ValiTest generates unittesting cases that testing or verification can use to confirm the property's validity.
